As for their source, it arises from various inversions.
One should not, one should not follow the path of the vile and accept the six perversions, which are called inversions of thought.
The reason one accepts them and does not abandon them is that they reside in the mental faculty and reside in form.
No, one does not abandon these various inversions; one maintains them within the mind.
Regarding form, it is the physical body; the preservation of the body is likewise so.
To conceive of the impure as pure through mental construction is permissible.
Once the mind has formed this thought, one finds pleasure in what is seen and experiences its departure; this is called a perversion of view.
"Listening" means to follow.
"Receiving what goes forth" means going forth to receive.
To follow what the deluded mind finds acceptable, to diligently fix it in thought, and to take pleasure in what the eyes see while going forth to receive various desires—this is called inverted view.
What he has seen serves as the sign (*nimitta*); through conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there arise twelve inversions (*viparyāsa*). What are the twelve?
There are three regarding the body (*kāya*), three regarding sensation (*vedanā*), three regarding the mind (*citta*), and three regarding phenomena (*dharma*).
There are four inversions of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), four inversions of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and four inversions of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
Furthermore, these occur when there is a meeting of conditions through the sense bases (*āyatana*) and forms (*rūpa*).
"Sense base" here means that form does not enter the eye, but the eye goes out to seek the form; this is what constitutes the meeting with form.
These constitute the twelve inversions:
three regarding the body, three regarding sensation, three regarding the mind, and three regarding phenomena, totaling twelve inversions.
Regarding the three pertaining to the body, they are: first, inversion of perception; second, inversion of intention; and third, inversion of view.
Within these inversions there are four inversions; as for the four inversions, taking the four things that are not eternal to be eternal constitutes the four inversions.
Thus, with these six, there are twelve links of dependent origination, which immediately entail the six sense bases.
Regarding the seventy-two inversions, they arise from causes and conditions obtained from the very beginning; according to the number of these causes and conditions, they are immeasurable.
Although there are seventy-two inversions, because they arise following causes and conditions, these inversions themselves are of immeasurable number.
That which is incalculable is not a number among people; there is no inversion regarding that which is incalculable.
When it arises in the minds of people, it is precisely an inversion.
Those five aggregates constitute the four bodies of existence.
The four bodies are the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*dharma*).
The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) combine to form the dharma-body.
All that belongs to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is subsumed under the body.
The aggregate of form is the body; the aggregate of sensation is the body; the aggregate of mind is the body.
From the existence of the aggregate of sensation, there belongs the body of sensation; from the existence of the aggregate of consciousness, there belongs the body of mind.
That which belongs to the body of mind refers to the aggregate of consciousness belonging to the mind.
From the aggregate of perception up to the aggregate of formations, these belong to the body of phenomena (*dharmakāya*).
As for the "body of phenomena," it refers to the sixfold factors within the body; it is also called "undergoing various dharmas of birth and death."
Based on the existence of these five aggregates (skandhas), one undergoes the causal conditions for the four bodies.
The "four bodies" refers to the four [types of] superior bodies.
"Causal conditions" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
Once the five aggregates exist, there are four bodies, which bring the twelve links of dependent origination to completion.
To reckon that body, which is impure, as pure is the perversion of the body;
to reckon that suffering as pleasure is the perversion of sensation.
To regard that which is impermanent as permanent is a perversion of mind;
to regard that which is not the self as the self is a perversion of phenomena.

In order to rectify these four perversions, the Buddha manifested the four foundations of mindfulness and taught their analytical distinctions: he taught the observation of the body as the body’s characteristics through the foundation of mindfulness, so that those who perceive impurity as pure and hold such a perversion may attain liberation.

The Buddha beheld that the minds of sentient beings were submerged in the abyss of blindness and ignorance; because they regarded what was crooked as straight and what was inverted as correct, he analytically taught the four foundations of mindfulness to enable them to contemplate.

A fragile vessel is truly difficult to preserve; those who are enlightened awaken first and immediately return from the thicket of the three realms. By purifying their minds and entering the state of non-existence, they are said to attain liberation from perversion.
He contemplates feelings as feelings; he resolves what is suffering to be happiness, thereby attaining liberation from that perversion.
He contemplates the mind as the mind; he resolves what is impermanent to be permanent, thereby attaining liberation from that perversion.
He contemplates phenomena as phenomena; he resolves what is not-self to be self, thereby attaining liberation from that perversion.
To be in darkness within darkness, as if unable to understand, is the mark of delusion (*moha*); it causes one to fall into states of inversion.

To desire to go toward that [darkness] is the mark of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); it causes one to undergo form for the sake of a body, leading to deception and wonderment, which is the mark of greed (*lobha*); it causes one to fall into taking what is not given.
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) is also [a secondary affliction].
Taking what is not given is theft.
Because of one's own body, to repeatedly harbor a deceitful mind toward others is called "deceiving with a deceitful countenance" (*śāṭhyarūpa*).
Without the eye of wisdom coming forth, the eye silently goes out to grasp forms; thus all six sense-faculties go forth, which is why it is called "taking what is not given.

That which is contrary to one's wishes is the mark of malice (*dveṣa*), which causes one to fall into the place of killing and constitutes the mark of ignorance (*moha*) regarding uncomprehending matters; this causes one to receive the false and fall into false states, performing the deeds of those who are preyed upon, and failing to reject the marks of receptivity.
This means that because the mind does not repel various evils and follows whatever it projects, one consequently undergoes the retribution of evil marks.
This serves to cause one to fall into the notion of permanence and to remain ignorant of the body.
The four great elements are called the body.
"Body" (軀) means the physical form (體). The physical form is the substance.
The six sense-faculties are called the "substance.
"Objects" refers to the thirty-six substances within the body.
To regard these as mutually meeting marks is to cause one to conceive the notion of pleasure; this constitutes falling into a state of attachment and a lack of understanding.
This means that the mind does not enter into the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment to comprehend them.

Regarding the characteristics of phenomena, one forms the notion of a self-body; this causes one to fall into the view that "this is I" and "this is mine. One falls into grasping at the marks of form and appearance, leading to the calculation that "this is pure," which in turn causes one to fall into failing to guard the sense faculties.
This refers to failing to guard and restrain the six sense faculties.
These constitute the nine categories, which have already been analyzed; thus, it has been explained that all such things are unfit to be associated with as unrighteous companions.
"Companion" refers to the companionship of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The eye has form as its companion; the same applies to the other six sense-faculties.
This is something that those who have heard much can understand.
Only those who have heard much and seen widely can understand this;
those who have not heard much will ultimately fail to understand.
"Ultimately" (卒) means "in the end" (遂).
Lacking extensive learning and broad vision, their practice becomes stunted and they ultimately fail to understand this.
This is something that the wise can comprehend, while the unwise cannot understand at all.
This means that a foolish person does not engage in extensive study or broad learning; thus, upon first hearing it, they ultimately fail to understand.
It is the learned who can understand.
That is to say, it is only those who are learned who are able to comprehend it.
If one does not abandon [these views], one will never understand this.
If one does not understand through non-observance, there are nine points of severance that cause all categories of pure dharmas to fall into a state of aggregation.
What are these nine?
First, cessation; second, contemplation; third, non-greed; fourth, non-anger; fifth, non-delusion; sixth, impermanence; seventh, suffering; eighth, non-self; ninth, impurity—these are the nine.
The Master said:
"To sever" means to cut off all evil intentions.

To attain the skill of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) is to be free from craving for worldly desires, to be without a mind of anger or delusion, and to realize the truths of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity.

That cessation is called *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness). Being able to cease, having ceased, correctly ceasing, gathering in cessation, not losing cessation, and being without mental aspiration—when the mind is tranquil and directed toward mindfulness one by one, this is called cessation. The Master says:

it means being able to cease while in the body; likewise, being able to cease immediately when in sensation (*vedanā*), in mind (*citta*), or in phenomena (*dharma*)—the mind does not form aspirations.

Right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) is subsumed under the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*); it gathers the six sense faculties into stillness, thereby attaining the concentrated mind (*samādhi-citta*).
"One-pointed mindfulness" refers to *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), wherein the six sense faculties are focused one-pointedly in every state.
What is contemplation? Contemplation is defined as the thorough understanding of the aggregates (skandhas).
The consciousness-principle is subtle, and the various aggregates are difficult to discern.
When one clearly realizes the principle, one should contemplate that within a single breath there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

That is to say, at the initial stage of counting the breaths, it is the wind-element, which is termed the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); when contemplating the breath, one fears that sensation (*vedanā*) will become the aggregate of suffering (*vedanā-skandha*).

When these two thoughts arise, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) extends from the breath to the act of perceiving; the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) follows; and once the mind is known through the breath, this constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
Thus, within a single breath, there are the five aggregates.
To discern and know the five aggregates is for the sake of understanding the aggregates;
it is for the sake of upholding them.
It is to maintain mastery over the six sense faculties.
In order to enter,
one must correctly abandon the six perversions so that they do not enter the six sense-faculties.
One must thoroughly understand names and realize their origin from the root.
The four formless aggregates (skandhas) constitute "name" (nāma), and the four great elements (mahābhūtas) constitute "form" (rūpa).

Regarding "arising from the root": this means that the root arises from the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); the five aggregates and the six [sense bases] arise from what is entered.
Having understood from the beginning, phenomena have already arisen.
Phenomena are the phenomena of birth and death;
one should understand this clearly.
One thoroughly understands suffering, thoroughly understands its origin, thoroughly understands its cessation, and thoroughly understands the path leading to its cessation.
That is to say, one who practices the path should clearly comprehend suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; this constitutes the thorough understanding of the Four Noble Truths.

One should thoroughly understand that wholesome states arise from the path, while unwholesome states arise from suffering and its origin; the seeker of the home-leaving life should clearly comprehend this.
Having understood increase, he increases it further;
he further increases the practice of the Path;
he understands the white and the black.
The Way is pure and white; the world is turbid and black.
Black signifies darkness.
One should clearly understand this and accordingly follow it.
This means that one may follow the path of the right conduct;
one must not follow it means that one must not follow the path of wrong conduct.
To discern and know these as the white and black classes:
this is what is meant by "discernment," namely, the discernment of the white and black classes according to the truths.
It is for the sake of "pulling. Pulling means pulling along; it signifies that the Way can be practiced.
It is not non-pulling.
This means that improper desire is not to be indulged in;
it is base.
Base, indeed, is the heavy burden of desire.
Descend further;
descend further. Contemplate what has been cultivated on the path; contemplate it again and again, being careful not to forget.
This is called mindfulness.
Mindfulness means counting the breaths.
To mindfully return to the source of the Way after having advanced is called "returning mindfulness" (fùniàn).
The *Ānāpāna* [Sūtra] states, "Mindfulness awakens the seeds of the mind"; this is what is meant.
It refers to contemplative reflection (*cintā-vipaśyanā*). That is to say, one constantly brings to mind whatever objects are being contemplated.
It is for the sake of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness means recollection; it refers to constantly recollecting and being aware of what one has already practiced while training.
It is for the sake of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Having attained the ultimate exhaustion [of defilements], there is nothing he does not know;
this constitutes his eye.
This eye is the Eye of the Path (mārga-cakṣus).
Having already attained the mind of the Way, there is nothing his eye does not see.
He acts as a counselor.
To "counsel" means to employ skillful means of benevolence and compassion.
To fulfill:
having observed it so that it has pervaded everywhere, he fulfills its hollows.
To liberate.
To understand the profundity of the Way and be liberated from the three realms is to possess wisdom and illumination.
To understand the profundity of the Way, cross over the three realms, and attain nothing that is not known is to possess all-encompassing vision.
Regarding the phrase "the profound wisdom and clarity" (*zhòngyún huìmíng*): this refers to it being the wisdom among wisdoms and the great illumination among illuminations.
Wisdom is termed the Dharma of Pure Wisdom; the meaning of this is likewise so.
This is for the sake of desire; desire is the path of desire.
His mind constantly delights in the practice of the Way.

It is called "Light" because, having perfected its mastery, the wisdom of liberation is luminous; those whose hearts delight in this Dharma universally bestow great compassion and moisture, their radiance pervading the ten directions so that all living beings receive its bounty—therefore, it is called "Light."
I dare not fail to remain detached.
Having already understood this, I dare not fail to remain detached from all worldly defilements;
I do so for the sake of contemplating the Dharma.
Dharma refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ).
They constitute the awakening of the mind.
Through self-awakening, one attains omniscience.
This constitutes right view.
"Right" refers to the Eightfold Right Path.
"View" refers to the track of the Way (the path).
They constitute the seeds of the Path.
Cultivating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment constitutes the lower seeds of the Path.
This is called contemplation.
There are also several types of contemplation for the two classes [of practitioners].
Having already awakened to and perceived them with the mind, they serve as the seeds for the lower path; therefore, they are called "contemplations.
As for the "several types for the two classes," this refers to the purity of the Path and worldly impurity; because their matters are manifold, they are called "several."
First is the contemplation of purity.
This refers to the contemplation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment within a secluded, tranquil, and pure environment; this is called the contemplation of purity.
Second is the contemplation of impurity.
Contemplating the three types of corpses constitutes the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). The three [remaining types] constitute the contemplation of purity (*viśuddhi-bhāvanā*).
This means that the cessation of mental activity is "clear" (*vi*) and the exhaustion of defilements is "pure" (*śuddhi*); therefore, it is called "purity."

The fourth is the contemplation of impurity; the fifth is the contemplation of black; the sixth is the contemplation of white; and the seventh is the contemplation of what is to be discarded (*vivarjanīya*).
Regarding "what is to be discarded": pure dharmas are to be discarded, as one contemplates karma as a treasure.
Eighth is the contemplation of the unwholesome; ninth is the contemplation of the transgression of sin.
Regarding the contemplation of the transgression of sin, it is the observation that treading upon the path of deviance leads one into the three evil realms, thereby deluding the mind.
Tenth is the contemplation of calamity and fortune.
This refers to observing and knowing which afflictions belong to misfortune or fortune.
The eleventh is the contemplation of bondage,
observing that the consciousness-spirit is bound within the twelve links of dependent origination.
Twelfth is the contemplation of liberation:
knowing that by relinquishing the twelve links of dependent origination, one shall attain liberation.
Thirteenth is the contemplation of that which is beneficial.
Having already attained liberation, one acts for the sake of benefiting others.
Fourteenth is the contemplation of loss, which is without benefit.
"Loss" refers to losing the path; it brings no benefit to oneself.
The fifteenth is the contemplation of going forth (*yāna-vipaśyanā*).

"Going forth" refers to the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) proceeding toward the six inversions (*ṣaḍ-viparyāsa*), perceiving [the objects] of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, tangibility, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
The sixteenth is the contemplation of returning (*āgama-vipaśyanā*).
Returning, one returns to contemplate the body.
Seventeenth is the contemplation of receiving retribution:
the formation of the twelve links of dependent origination constitutes the receiving of retribution.
Eighteenth is the contemplation for the removal of offenses.
One contemplates the severance of the twelve links of dependent origination in order to remove offenses;
therefore, it is called "contemplation."
There are also two reasons for this teaching that "cessation alone is everything.
All people in the world have two kinds of illnesses. What are these two?
The first is delusion and the second is craving.
Because there are these two maladies, the Buddha manifests two medicines. What are these two?
First is cessation (śamatha) and second is insight (vipaśyanā).
If one employs these two medicines, the two diseases will be cured.
Cessation and insight are the two medicines; delusion and craving are the two diseases.
The Buddha cures two maladies through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which is called "healing the disease.
He causes one to realize this for oneself:
*śamatha* extinguishes craving and *vipaśyanā* extinguishes delusion; with the extinction of delusion, one attains the realization of the Path.
Craving and desire no longer arise;
when the path of cessation and insight is fulfilled, delusion and attachment are extinguished.
One who is satiated by the Way does not hunger for the mundane—this is what is meant by "no longer craving."
When mindfulness brings about liberation of the mind and delusion has been dispelled, one attains liberation through wisdom.
One attains the four noble truths of the impermanent, which are direct, pure, and stainless; thus, having no further aspiration for the three realms, this is called liberation.
*Śarīra-skandha-dhātv-āyatana-sūtra*, Volume Upper;
*Śarīra-skandha-dhātv-āyatana-sūtra*, Volume Lower. This sūtra contains many instances of the character "𧗪" (shēng), which in other editions is all rendered as "行" (xíng).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
What is the medicine for that craving? It is cessation. When craving has ceased, the mind is liberated.
When the mind is liberated, the illness is healed.
Craving is the disease; cessation is the medicine.
What is that medicine for delusion?
It is contemplation.
Once delusion has been dispelled through understanding, one proceeds from wisdom to liberation; this constitutes the healing of the disease.
Thus the Buddha said:
"These two dharmas should be known: first, name; second, form.
These two dharmas should be abandoned: first, ignorance; second, craving."
Regarding "delusion and craving": the four aggregates (*skandhas*) constitute the name, and the four great elements (*mahābhūtas*) constitute the form.
Within the combined body, there is nothing but delusion and craving.
As for names and designations, the practitioner should employ *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to investigate and eliminate them.
There are two dharmas that one should know for oneself:
first, wisdom; second, liberation.
There are two dharmas that can be cultivated: first, tranquility; second, insight.
Having stilled [the mind], one causes consciousness to cognize form; having cognized it, one causes craving to attain relinquishment.
By knowing that the four great elements constitute the object of consciousness, the mind then does not become stained by form.
That which is unstained by form does not fall into longing; therefore, it is said that consciousness of form causes craving to attain relinquishment.
When craving has been understood, the mind then attains liberation; one realizes for oneself that it has come to rest.
When practice is fulfilled, one then attains the relinquishing of delusion.
When the cessation of proliferation is fulfilled, one then attains the relinquishing of delusion.
Having already abandoned delusion, one attains liberation through wisdom and realizes it for oneself.
If a bhikṣu has already mastered these two dharmas—namely, knowing both name and form—and has already mastered these two dharmas—namely, abandoning both delusion and craving.
Thus, up to this point, there is no further attachment, and one’s practice should be considered complete.
This means that through the cessation of both insight (*vipaśyanā*) and tranquility (*śamatha*), delusion and craving are eliminated; this constitutes the completion of the task.
Yet, if one wishes to transcend the world, it is because there still remains a residue of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) that has not yet been transcended.
"Those who have not yet crossed over by means of the unconditioned" refers to those who have already attained *nirvāṇa*,
but for whom it has not yet been proclaimed. "The unconditioned is complete" refers to those who have already attained *nirvāṇa*.
When life has reached its end and is completed—
meaning one no longer undergoes the lifespan of birth and death—
then suffering is exhausted, ensuring that there shall be no further suffering hereafter.

Since those aggregates, which were both grasped and included, have been exhausted, stilled, and brought to cessation, there will subsequently be no further aggregates to be grasped or included; being without connection, they shall not arise again.
This means that when evil intentions are extinguished, they no longer give rise to birth and death;
this is called "without remainder.
It means that evil intentions are completely extinguished without even the slightest residue remaining.

Having already attained transcendence and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), these constitute the two types of unconditioned seeds; they do not crave even pure fundamental nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). Why is this so?
Within the three realms, one neither attains, nor hopes for, nor seeks anything.
Having already attained the three concentrations, the six sense faculties no longer seek or pursue anything within the three realms; this is called the "pure essence."
This is called the root of purity through non-attachment.
For whom is this root?
It is for the purity of the body through non-attachment.
Regarding "purity," it is also fundamentally based on the mental attention toward other associated pure dharmas.
This means that there is no further arising of deviance, and that which is mentally attended to consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*).
This is the root of purity through non-attachment.
There is also a root of purity which the Buddha has taught as being eight kinds of practice;
these constitute the three types of pure paths, and this is the root of non-attachment.
What are the three?
First is right effort as a remedy; second is right mindfulness; third is right concentration. These are the roots of the three kinds of pure paths.
Therefore, this is called the root of purity: non-greed.
What is the root of non-ill will and non-transgression of the Dharma? It is as follows:

if one endures what provokes anger, one will not give rise to ill will in the future; through the causal condition of patience, one becomes free from ill will; being free from ill will, one does not undergo calamity; thus, there is no ill will, no hatred, and one does not hate.
Where there is ill will, there is immediate anger; where there is no ill will, there is no anger.
To be without resentment and not to harbor resentment is to be without ill will and not to transgress the root of the Dharma.
Therefore, this is called the root of the dharma of non-anger and non-transgression.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of pure paths: first, the root of the dharma of non-anger and non-transgression as right speech; second, as right action; and third, as right livelihood.
This means that for one who has attained the Way, it constitutes the attainment of benefit.

From the stage of physical and mental exertion upward, one takes up the eightfold path; furthermore, from the initial arousal of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of the Way, this is also called the attainment of benefit.
These are the three kinds of pure paths to enlightenment.
Therefore, they are called the root of the dharma of non-anger and non-transgression.
What is that root of purity which is free from delusion?

By means of wisdom, one perceives the Four Truths as they truly are; as they truly are, one should undergo purification, being neither deluded nor confused, not following after confusion, and not falling into confusion.
That is to say, by attaining the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one ultimately does not fall into these various matters of confusion.
The clear manifestation of wisdom is seeing its own characteristics.
This means that the elimination of the three poisons constitutes the clarity of wisdom, while penetrating the Eightfold Noble Path constitutes seeing its characteristics.
Proceeding from the dharma of purity, this is the fundamental source of non-delusion and purity.
To whom does this "root" belong?

It belongs to one who is not deluded regarding the body, speech, and mind that are pure; it is the mental attention to the characteristics of the pure dharmas that are interconnected, recollecting the root of those dharmas.
The fundamental dharmas are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
They also serve as the basis for non-delusion by way of two kinds of pure paths: first, right view; second, right intention. These constitute the basis for the two kinds of pure paths.
Therefore, this is called the root of purity free from delusion.
These constitute the three purities; as for the eightfold path, they are already categorized according to their respective applications.
The character "fen" (份) is pronounced like the "fen" in "fenbu" (分部).
In accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, one should practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
"Impermanence" is thus; that is the perception of impermanence. What is it like?
All that is clung to is the perception of impermanence; that which is perceived and reckoned as known is sensation (*vedanā*).
Once there is perception and reckoning, one immediately knows for oneself and subsequently acts without ceasing; this constitutes sensation.
This is the perception of impermanence.
It also arises from the eight worldly dharmas. What are these eight?
If there is gain,
the householder’s mind, which has obtained the benefit of the ultimate offering, will not be joyful. If there is no gain...
To cultivate virtue yet have it diminished by accumulated burdens is called "lack of benefit.
Renown: when the fragrance of one's virtue spreads far and wide, it is called "renown."
"He is not renowned.
Although his virtues are complete and his character lofty, he is obstructed by the various wicked ones; thus, they say he is "unrenowned.
There is a discourse on this.
Pure and detached, he was falsely slandered by a faction; this is called "discourse.
He did not engage in such discourse.
His virtue was so lofty that it suppressed slander, yet he did not become arrogant because of it.

If one plants one's will in the Way while enduring suffering, yet hardships and calamities follow one after another— whether it be the disaster of total annihilation or the sins of the three miserable realms— this is called "suffering."
If one delights in attaining the glory of a celestial king and fulfilling one's heart's desires, this is called pleasure;
yet the mind remains neither falling into nor accepting such states.
This is to fall away from pleasure.
To dwell in prosperity without arrogance, to remain steadfast without falling into decline, to not be dazzled by the displays of the wicked and clever,
and for the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) to remain unaffected— finding no joy in gain and no sorrow in loss.
The *Dharmādarśa-sūtra* states: "One is not shaken by gain or loss, defamation or praise, honor or reproach, suffering or pleasure.
This is the aspiration of pure concentration.
One does not accept certain thoughts; through the cultivation of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), one attains the cessation of unwholesome thoughts.
Guarding and observing ensures that one does not lose composure.
"Cessation" means ceasing to accept those aforementioned discursive thoughts.
Because these two intentions are [defiled], evil ceases.
This is called the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
What is that perception of suffering (*dukkhasaññā*)?
To engage in all worldly activities is suffering.
That which is conceived, perceived,
and felt— namely, the knowledge that one has experienced suffering— is what must be recognized and extinguished by the practitioner.
This is called the perception of suffering.
From this, what follows?
One regards the perception of suffering as already practiced, already increased, and frequently cultivated.
All sufferings increase from habitual accumulation.
One becomes insatiable due to greed;
greed arises from the myriad things, longing arises from peril, hatred arises from jealousy, delusion arises from a lack of inquiry, and ignorance arises from darkness.
Covetousness, anger, and delusion constitute the "feet.
This is so that one does not fall into covetousness.
It is said that through covetousness a person undergoes aging; through anger, illness; and through delusion, death.
Because they arise from merit, those who have already attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment do not fall into greed.
This is because their minds do not accept [defilements] and thus do not fall; they are mutually restrained so as not to fall.
"Drawing forth" (qian) means "to connect.
It refers to the continuous succession of the path and its intent, ensuring that one does not fall into birth and death.
Do not dwell upon [these thoughts].
One does not harbor evil thoughts.
Guarding one's various intentions and contemplating them as already being evil leads to cessation.
One's own virtue consists in restraining the six sense-faculties from evil.
Having attained tranquility, one attains both tranquility and insight.
From this, one contemplates and aspires to achieve this essential point.
What is that which is not a perception of the body?
Regarding all dharmas, one does not reckon them as a body and does not fall into the notion of a body.
It is said that among all the dharmas of the four great elements, one does not reckon them as a body.
The body is an impermanent thing; the enlightened person does not fall into the conceptualization of a body.
To perceive and cognize what is perceived and felt is called the perception of non-self.
From this, what arises?
Once one has attained the perception of non-self, through mindfulness and reflection, it increases until it causes one to conceive of this [state] as "I."
"This is this" refers to one's own reckoning that "this is my body.
To be thus, one must not accept the mind; one abandons various states—these "states" refer to the eighty-four states.
Having spoken thus, one realizes the eighty-four modes [of mental activity] and immediately abandons them without accepting them.
Non-acceptance and non-abiding constitute contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); through this, afflictions are brought to cessation.
"Non-acceptance and non-abiding" means not abiding in the breath.
The reason one is able to repel the eighty-four states [of distraction] is precisely that one attains the cessation of the mind through the contemplation of impurities (aśubha-bhāvanā).
This constitutes the essential path to realization; as for this "essential," it means that the practice of the perception of non-self (*anātman-saṃjñā*) is the essential path to realization.
What is that perception of foulness?
It is the perception that all things in the world are foul; whatever one perceives and personally experiences as foul, this is called the perception of foulness.
From this perception, what kind of aspiration is attained?

Having cultivated the perception of impurity, one becomes mindful, reflective, and increasingly refined; one causes the mind to withdraw from and abandon the five worldly pleasures, so that the mind is no longer drawn away, does not grasp, and no longer falls into various discursive thoughts, thereby attaining protection.
By means of this, one attains stability.
This is what is meant by "reaching the essential goal.
Reaching the essential goal consists of forming the mental intention of the perception of impermanence.
He possesses four modes of thought and mindfulness.
Regarding the four modes of thought, he contemplates the four dhyānas.
Regarding mindfulness, he maintains non-distraction through the abandonment [of hindrances].
Why is this? It is to cause one to know the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
That is to say, by attaining the four dhyānas, one immediately knows from whence the five aggregates arise.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke of this as "discriminative view.
That perception of impurity is a contemplation intended to bring about liberation from the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

This means that the foul secretions of the four great elements all belong to form; by contemplating the impurities within the body, one repels desire for form, and thus it is said to be "liberation through this."
That perception of suffering causes the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) to be liberated from this [craving].
When one perceives the body as suffering, the aggregate of sensation is extinguished.
That perception of non-self causes the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) to be likewise liberated from this [craving].
Attaining the mindfulness that there is no self-body means that the perceptions of the two aggregates [feeling and perception] are extinguished.

That which is not the conceptualization of permanence causes the aggregate of consciousness to be liberated from this; consciousness recognizes that all phenomena are impermanent, and thus the mind does not harbor greedy attachment—hence it is called "the liberation of consciousness."
He proceeds from stillness and cessation.
"Cessation" (zhi) means gathering-in (she).
Gathering the six sense-faculties back so that the mind no longer receives external objects—this is the perception of cessation.
He causes craving to be liberated from this;
he causes it to be liberated from this through the contemplation of loathsomeness. He causes delusion to be liberated from this;
he brings about the relinquishing of craving through non-greed.
Having abandoned the mind of craving for flowers, not even a trace remains.
From non-anger, he abandons anger;
from non-delusion, he abandons delusion.
From the perception of impermanence, he causes them to understand permanence;
from the perception of suffering, he causes them to understand pleasure;
from the perception of non-self, he causes them to understand the self.
From that perception of impurity, he seeks to resolve the perception of purity.
From that restraint through tranquility, his mind is able to attain withdrawal; this is the perception of tranquility, which causes him to proceed from this to the dhyāna of tranquility.
"Stopping" (śamatha) means "stabilizing.
It stabilizes the mind within the four dhyānas.

When one follows all phenomena in their profound stillness and is able to attain liberation and receptivity, this is called contemplative visualization (vipaśyanā), which causes the mind to stabilize and dwell upon all-knowing wisdom.
From contemplation one attains stillness; contemplating and discerning all things is for the sake of abiding in omniscience.

From desire one can attain the thought of returning [to the source]; this is the characteristic of non-greed, which causes one to cease from taking what is not given. Form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and improper thoughts are termed "taking what is not given."

Having attained the fourth dhyāna, one returns the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and no longer experiences the six external desires; therefore, it is said that one "returns from taking what is not given.
Thereafter, delusion does not arise again; this constitutes the absence of the perception of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃjñā*), which causes one to return from killing.
To attain cessation regarding both phenomena and objects is the characteristic of non-delusion; it is for the sake of attaining cessation, wherein one ceases that which is clung to by the world.
To take dharmas as objects and be able to receive their characteristics is the perception of impermanence; it causes one to know arising from birth and to know extinction from death.
As for "arising from," it arises from craving.
One who knows understands its source of arising and understands that which can extinguish it.
Consciousness is this locus; consciousness is the locus of the three poisons.

For the sake of the world’s craving, one creates the world’s renewed existence; that which is perceived through ideation is suffering, and that which is conceived through thought is the locus for the seeds of pain. All phenomena do not abide in ideation; this is the non-self ideation, this is the ideation of thought. Having seen the corpse of the body already decayed and bloated blue, one takes up these signs as objects of perception.
This refers to what was stated above regarding the perception of the signs of death;
this constitutes the contemplation of impurity.
By focusing one's thoughts upon these signs, it is described as the contemplation of impurity.
From this point on, one repents and causes [the mind] to rest in tranquility.
This constitutes the detailed explanation of the views established within the nine grades;
it manifests the nine severances.
This constitutes the entire category of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That is to say, the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is explained as being complete with its attendants; by whom is this known?
Those who have heard much or heard little do not thereby become wise.

Lacking wisdom, they do not abide in the permanent; their minds are fixed upon the sūtras, and because their intentions are thus linked together, they fail to engage in non-conceptual contemplation, which prevents them from attaining the perception of impermanence.
They do not accept the perception of impermanence, causing them to fall from this into the five pleasures and be shrouded by those five pleasures.

They cause one to lose what ought to be cultivated, fail to understand the perception of suffering, fall into the grasping of the five aggregates, and cause the mind to reckon that this body—which is fundamentally not a single entity—is composed of many parts.

Without abandoning or observing [the body], one causes [the mind] not to fall into the perception that it is not the body; because the mind is intent upon the pleasure of its appearance, one reckons this body as pure and does not reckon it as being covered by skin and flesh, thereby causing one not to fall into the perception of impurity and not to dwell in sensation.
The fool does not accept this inverted perception.
It is simply that he lacks faith in it; by causing him to be without perception and not to accept joy, these four types [of perceptions] are thereby eliminated.
There are four kinds, namely the four types of non-permanence.

Having entered the stage of attaining the category of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the Buddha taught that a bhikṣu who wishes to see and know with faith should seek to abide in the four streams of entry as the dharma of purification.
Regarding the six matters of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), one attains mindfulness as purity, thereby falling into the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
One does not abandon the characteristics of skillful means (*upāya-lakṣaṇa*) so as to bring about purity.
Arising from purity, one causes [the mind] to fall into the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

The Buddha taught that a bhikṣu who wishes to see and know the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*) should attend to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) regarding what has been experienced in the past.
Furthermore, there are the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
By recollecting their characteristics without forgetting, one gives rise to non-forgetfulness and enters the four foundations of mindfulness.
The Buddha said that if a bhikṣu wishes to see and know through mindfulness, he should contemplate it within the four foundations of mindfulness.
To have a single-pointed mental focus is concentration; arising from non-delusion, it causes one to fall into the stage of the four dhyānas.
The Buddha said that if a bhikṣu wishes to know the faculty of concentration, he should know it to reside within the four dhyānas.

Counting the breath is the application of mindfulness to the body; following the breath is the application of mindfulness to sensations; cessation is the application of mindfulness to the mind; and observation is the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
When these four applications of mindfulness are established, the five aggregates are brought to rest; this is called "returning."
Purification through returning is that which corresponds to the four dhyānas.
Calculating from the root, this constitutes wisdom; as for one who is able to attain "retention" (dhāraṇī), it is retention that sustains the six sense faculties.
From this, one initiates [the process] so as to cause entry into the Four Noble Truths.
By means of great wisdom and the dhāraṇī that governs the six sense faculties, one causes the mind to descend into the Four Noble Truths.
The Buddha said that if a bhikṣu who possesses the faculty of wisdom wishes to see [the truth], he must abide in the Four Noble Truths.
Therein lie four wheels:
These are the wheel of dwelling in excellent commanderies and counties, the wheel of relying on wise people, the wheel of one's own original right vows, and the wheel of merit from past lives.
As for "wheel," it is a metaphor for a chariot wheel, which is able to carry things to their destination.
It is said that when a person possesses these four wheels, they likewise carry them to the Way.
The four wheels correspond to the Four Noble Truths;
the four dhyānas serve as the vehicle for proceeding along the Way.
The "one hundred dharmas" and the "four wheels" have the same meaning.

These constitute the characteristics of dwelling together in virtue and the Way; this is what is meant by residing in a favorable district and county, enabling one to find a place where worthy persons may take refuge.
By attaining the characteristic of relying upon the Way and its Virtue (dharma), one is said to rely on a person of wisdom; from this, one falls into a state of right aspiration.
By attaining the characteristic of right aspiration, one is said to have right aspiration in body, which causes one to fall into a state of merit.
That which arises from the characteristics of entering into pure conduct is called merit; it causes one to fall into the five realms of pleasure.
That is to say, the five sense faculties constitute the five realms of pleasure.
These constitute the eleven fundamental bases of the dharma of precepts.
The first is that one who maintains the precepts for the sake of physical form will have no regret.
"Physical form" refers to the body.
First, one maintains the precepts of the body and does not commit the seven evils.
Second, one ensures that there is no regret within oneself, thereby causing the mind to attain joy.
This means that because the body does not commit evil, it causes the mind to be joyful.
Third, because joy already exists, it causes craving to arise.
Fourth, because the mind has already attained craving, the body attains tranquility (*praśrabdhi*).
Fifth, because the body has already attained tranquility, one immediately attains bliss; as for "tranquility," it refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
One attains happiness; one attains the happiness of the Path.
Sixth, when one’s mind has attained happiness, one then attains right stillness (*samyak-sthiti*).
Seventh, when one’s mind has attained right stillness, one then knows things as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*).
Eighth, having known things as they truly are, one becomes tranquil.
Ninth, being already tranquil, one attains detachment;
one detaches from the darkness of the five aggregates.
Tenth, having already attained detachment, one then attains liberation.
Eleventh, having already attained liberation, one then perceives wisdom;
that is to say, having already understood impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, one possesses wisdom regarding existence.
Possessing wisdom, one then knows that birth and death have come to an end.
With the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination, birth and death are exhausted.
Having completed the path of cultivation and finished all that was to be done, one no longer returns to undergo suffering.
To attain the three kinds of liberation is called "completion" (bi); to purify conduct, fulfill the precepts, and exhaust the outflows of the mind is called "conclusion" (jing).
One enters directly into nirvana, no longer returning to the triple world to undergo manifold sufferings.
What are the characteristics of the precepts?
To maintain the precepts until the end of one's life causes one to attain a body free from remorse.
Not increasing the characteristics of transgression constitutes being without remorse; from this, one attains joy, leading to the attainment of a state of joy.
The aspect of being agreeable is joy (*muditā*), which leads to the state of endearment; the aspect of contentment is the state itself.
"Contentment" (*tuṣṭi*) means fulfillment.
It leads to the state of reliance (*praśrabdhi*).
One relies upon the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
From the perspective of the practitioner, these constitute the characteristic of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), which brings about a state of bliss.
Once freedom from affliction constitutes the characteristic of bliss, one thereby attains a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Attaining the state of concentration" means abiding in the state of concentration that has been attained.
One explanation states:

having eliminated unwholesome thoughts, one attains the state where wholesome thoughts abide; the mind follows its tendencies without forgetting, which constitutes the characteristic of concentration.
The power of the Path can restrain the mind, causing it not to forget.
It leads one to reach the state of true wisdom; being free from delusion regarding what truly exists, and following along with this reality, this constitutes the state of tranquility.
If one knows that there is no self, this is the mark of tranquility.
When one attains the mindfulness of non-self, the mind becomes tranquil and concentrated.
This causes one to reach the state of separation from marks; not approaching or associating with them constitutes separation from marks.
When the mind is pure, one is separated from defilement; when virtue is far-reaching, one does not encounter evil.
Having thereby attained liberation, one is not harmed by unrighteousness and shall not suffer calamity.
If one attains the stage of non-retrogression or the stream-entry path (srotāpatti), one will no longer undergo the retribution of past misdeeds within the great mountains.
This is the mark of liberation, which brings about the wisdom of liberation; this "wisdom of vision" is the wisdom that perceives the Four Noble Truths.
There are four grounds of the path of virtue.
What are the four? They are the merit of the four types of practitioners.
If one possesses such knowledge and wisdom—
meaning that while worldly people know only the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), the practitioner knows the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni)—
this constitutes the ground of vision and the attainment of the tracks of the Path. These tracks of the Path refer to the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
This is the merit of attaining the Way.
To have suchness and such-like knowledge is to cast away and distance oneself from evil.
One who possesses such-like knowledge speaks of things as they truly are and knows the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

Having already understood the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, their intention becomes pure; they then loathe what is received through the six sense-faculties and seek to distance themselves from the three realms.
This is called the Stage of Thinness (tanubhūmi), wherein there is the merit of coming and going.
"Coming and going" refers to the stage where a Sakṛdāgāmin dwells.
That the three poisons are diminished is explained in the *Ānāpāna* [Sūtra].
Therein, the rejection of evil is treated as non-utility.
Evil—evil is the body.
To not employ it, and not to employ worldly glory;
this is called the stage of detachment.
Having already become detached from those [defilements], this is what is called "the merit of non-return.
Because they do not return— namely, as *anāgāmins* (Non-returners)—
and are born forever in the heavens without returning to the human realm, they are called "Non-returners."
This is called the completion of the stage of desire.
As for the meaning of "merit that is both unattached and non-arising," what is its significance?
What is the purport of this question?
The disciples of the Way have eight kinds of those who cultivate the path (mārga-kāraka).
That is to say, the first four types cultivate the purity of the path and all attain entry into the cultivation of the path.
These are called "those who cultivate," which constitutes merit; therefore, they are called "the merit of those who cultivate."
Why is this? Because it is called "merit" by virtue of being pure; this is pure merit, and this is the Way and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*).
There are eight kinds of pure paths of merit which constitute this merit; therefore, it is called "pure merit."
He is one who ought to attain the path of the tracks.
How so? Because he has already attained the path associated with the truths.
Having already attained the path of the tracks, one is in correspondence with the Four Noble Truths.
The disciple then severs the three fetters.
What are those three fetters?
First, to know that the body is not the self; second, to be free from doubt; third, not to barter or trade the precepts.
The practitioner who upholds the precepts attains these three modes of livelihood, masters the state of non-ideation, and brings salvation to those within the three realms.
One does not trade this precept for the glory and pleasure of the heavens.

Having severed these three fetters, the disciple on the path falls into the stream of the Dharma; no longer falling into the evil realms, and having undergone seven more births among gods and humans, one severs suffering wherever one goes through coming and going, attaining liberation from suffering.
This refers to the stream-enterer (srotāpanna), who after seven deaths and seven births attains the stage of the Arhat.
This is called the "ground of vision" (darśana-bhūmi), which constitutes the merit of attaining the tracks of the Path.
The "ground of vision" is the ground of the path of vision (darśana-mārga).
What is that? It is for the sake of causing the mind to descend [into realization]: "This body also knows this body. Question:
By what means does the mind come to have a body, such that it considers it to exist?
Answer: The five aggregates cause delusion.
Ignorance arises from not hearing [the Dharma].

For those in the world who do not see or awaken to it, nor receive instruction and precepts from one who has heard it, and for those who have heard it but have not yet discerned the manifestation of the True Dharma, they conceive of form as the body; they perceive form everywhere as the body, thinking, "This form is the body," and "Form is my body. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also explained as above.

Having thus attained this contemplation, one experiences the five pleasures. This attainment of contemplation refers to the foolish person with false views who, falling into the five aggregates as a self, takes delight in the five desires as pleasure.
The *Liaoben* says: "To cause one to doubt while already within doubt is precisely what is required;
the Buddha calls this 'delusion' (*moha*). This is its meaning.
It causes one to receive this body.
The fool considers the five pleasures to be glory, delighting in the perception of the body.
Thus, abandoning this body to take up another, he revolves in suffering;
he is one who has fallen into the body.
"Fallen" means submerged;
the mind is submerged within the body,
causing the mind to think, "I am this."
"This is it; this is the body.
What I have seen is real, it is authentic, and its truth is such.
Because I am bound by attachment to these marks, I do not attain mastery; I am dragged along by these marks in this manner, and thus there is that which I must endure."
The fool may simply consider that which he personally esteems to be right;
bound by worldly attachments, he follows the cycle of birth and death, enduring a multitude of transgressions without feeling any shame in his countenance.
That which the mind approves is what is accepted; once accepted, one follows it with attachment.
That which is approved is approved by the ignorant mind, and one immediately accepts it.
The mind is the head of attachment.
This constitutes wrong view, by which one falls into receiving this body.
One with wrong view perceives the body of the five aggregates as "I" and "mine.
Because they hold these five kinds of wrong views, they fall into the doubt that [the self] does not exist.
This refers to the view that there are no Three Jewels, nor is there any retribution for sin or merit. What are the five?
If one is affected by form, one perceives this body as being inferior to what preceded it.
Compared to the former, the five aggregates have already been explained;

the remaining three—perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are likewise [to be understood]. These constitute five false views that cause one to fall into the view of non-existence (*uccheda*);
the subsequent fifteen lead one to fall into the view of permanence (*śāśvata*).

Not only does one fall into the notion of permanence (*śāśvata-saṃjñā*) instead of the notion of non-existence, but by thus seeing that this body has already been severed, one abandons the sixty-two false views (*dṛṣṭi-gata*).
That is to say, for one who has attained the Path, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are severed; once the five aggregates are severed, the sixty-two false views are extinguished.

This prevents one from falling into the views of permanence or impermanence; having abandoned both the impermanent and the permanent, the disciples of the Way are free from inverted false views and are solely intent on transcending the world.
Now, as for the cessation of the five aggregates, all thoughts are stilled and exhausted, and there is no longer any perception of impermanence or permanence.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "You who are without thought now behold the *prajñāpāramitā*.
What is meant by *prajñāpāramitā*? It is that which brings about transcendence from the world.
What is the direct vision like?
It causes one not to fall into a body of false views.
If a disciple of the Way hears this—
hearing of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment— and practices them, they shall attain deliverance.
It constitutes right view, seeing through the various scriptural traditions—
just as Ānanda was able to penetrate the Buddha’s twelvefold division of scriptures.
It means that one has already attained the world-transcending unconditioned state and has already understood the world-transcending Dharma.
To understand the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is to be liberated from worldly dharmas.

One no longer perceives this form as the body; rather, one universally perceives form as the body, such that this form is both the body and its color, and this form is also my own body. This same [realization] applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, which are no longer perceived in such a manner.
Thus it is, as previously described.

Regarding the harm of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), for one who attains the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the five aggregates are immediately extinguished, and the three lower fetters (*trīṇy avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*) are completely liberated.
He then severed the three fetters (saṃyojana).
These fetters arise with such rapidity that they are beyond counting.
What are these three?
First is not seeing this body; second is the absence of anger; third is the absence of doubt.
Having attained these, the disciple of the Way becomes free from doubt.
When defilements are exhausted and great clarity arises, the doubts of the multitude are resolved.
There is also no doubt regarding the Buddha.
Regarding "regarding the Buddha": the Buddha is most exalted and supreme; as for his immeasurable pure conduct, the disciples likewise have no doubt about it.
Thus the verse says: "Having nothing further to purify, one begins with neither doubt nor wavering.
The meaning is exactly as this.
To have faith and to have joy—this is what it means to be a Buddha.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having perfected the practice of wisdom, dwells in bliss.
The severance of birth and death and the orientation toward the gate of Nirvāṇa—this is called bliss.
Having understood the world, he declares that his work of teaching and transforming the world is complete; those who were to be saved have been saved, with none remaining.
There is no dharma superior to this; he who masters this dharma acts as a teacher accordingly.
"Yù (to restrain) means to stop.
Fǎsuí (following the Dharma) means to follow the Dharma with diligence. As for 'instruction':

among all that is above and below in heaven and earth, the Buddha is the most supreme. To attain faith without doubt is to follow this Dharma with diligence; it is to be without fetters or doubts regarding the Dharma, and to possess faith and joy. The Buddha says that this Dharma can be learned and realized in the present."
This means that one can attain the Path.
It is evident through personal experience; it is said that the Buddha perceives all matters of good and evil, and thus he is seen by people.
Once understanding has become wisdom (*prajñā*), that which was previously craved, hungered for, and closely pursued is now severed.
Human nature craves the six objects of the senses; those who have realized the Way have already severed these cravings.
To "follow what has been severed" means not to follow the six emotions.
Emptiness has nothing with which to correspond.
One empties the mind and purifies the interior; because the will is at variance with desire (*rāga*), it is called "non-correspondence," meaning non-correspondence with the depraved.
Whether one attains or does not attain [reception], one does not receive desire.
Craving has already been destroyed;
having been destroyed, it is exhausted.
This means that craving and desire have already come to an end.

Having already detached and exhausted [defilements], one is free from craving and the wish for their cessation; having no aspiration for the three realms, this is called the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).
It is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This means that by being free from desire and having a mind of tranquility, one is without the perception of the three realms.
The *Dharmādarśa-sūtra* states: "If one does not harbor the intention to seek nirvāṇa, how much less could there be the perception of toil?"
This is what is meant by "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
By this, there is the second absence of fetters (*saṃyojana*):
first, hunger and thirst; second, their mutual extension.
Compared to the second fetter, this is non-existence; it is the absence of the fetters of the twelve links of dependent origination and the five aggregates.
There is no doubt.
This means that once the fetters are already untied, one has no doubts whatsoever regarding the True Dharma.
One attains practice in accordance with the Dharma.
"Dharma" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness;
"in accordance with" means practicing in conformity with them.
For the sake of the assembly of fellow students, for those who are without fetters and without doubt, there is already feeling and joy.
As for feeling, it is the experiencing of the factors of the path.
Experiencing in this way, the disciple who has attained the Path constitutes the assembly of learners.

"Assembly" (*saṃgha*) means gathering; it refers to the gathering of those with like-minded aspirations who, together with their peers throughout the three realms, seek to learn how to return to the fundamental non-being.

"Right reception" (*samyak-samādāna*) means that once one has received the precepts as appropriate, established meditative concentration, perfected wisdom, attained liberation, and accomplished the wisdom of liberation, these qualities become manifest and are brought to fulfillment.
"Right reception of the fruits" refers to receiving the fruits of cessation.

As with the following matters, one receives them in accordance with them—namely, the matters of precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; "fruits" here refers to right reception.
These are the disciples of the Buddha.
When these groups are gathered together as four pairs, following from those four pairs, they are called the "Eightfold Path of the Noble Ones" (āryapudgala).

As for the four pairs and eight individuals: this refers to those who have attained the fruit of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and those progressing toward it; those who have attained the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) and those progressing toward it; those who have attained the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmin) and those progressing toward it; and those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry (srotāpatti) and those progressing toward it. These are what are known as the four pairs and eight individuals.
They are esteemed and honored by the world;
that is to say, these eight persons are esteemed by the wise of the world, who love, revere, and honor them.
They are peerless, worthy of offerings, worthy of service, and worthy of respect; there is no ground for merit superior to this, for they are served both by devas and by humans.
To worship deities in hopes of receiving blessings, none is equal to making offerings to these eight holy ones; its merit is great.
This is the third. The third refers to the *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner).
He has already attained the state of one beyond doubt.

The *Anban jie* (Explanation of Ānāpāna) states: "The Sakṛdāgāmin, while remaining within the fruit of the desire realm, has already abandoned the four broad inversions and is free from all remaining doubts and fetters."
Following the pursuit of phenomena, all pursuits constitute suffering;
the pursuit of calamity and misfortune constitutes suffering.
Having already eliminated doubt and fetters, having already attained and rejoiced, [suffering] arises from craving as its condition.
Upon believing the Buddha’s words, the knots are immediately untied and one receives the joy of the Dharma; to cherish this without weariness constitutes practice.
Practice is the practice of the Way.
The Way is the attainment of the Way.
Suffering also arises from the habituation of craving;
suffering is born of desire.
That one does not know suffering for what it is as suffering is because of its long-standing habituation.

Having no more fetters of doubt, having received, understood, and rejoiced, with craving exhausted—this is the end of suffering. Thus, being without doubt and without fetters, having attained this reception, one attains joy; with craving exhausted, this is the end of suffering and the absence of fetters of doubt; having understood the reception, one attains joy.

Regarding the eightfold path, one practices it from this point onward so that suffering may be exhausted; thus, there is no doubt. When there is no doubt, the fetters do not arise again, and through liberation, one attains joy.
If one originally had doubts—whether regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha—one remains unliberated.
"Fundamental" means "past lives.
Whatever doubts I had regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha have now all been resolved, and I no longer harbor any doubt.

If there were originally doubts concerning suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—should there have been any lingering doubts in past lives regarding these Four Noble Truths—they have now all been resolved.
That which is deluded by [ignorance] and not understood, following the inclinations of one's doubts—this is thus. What is this "wound"?

It is that which has already been understood and fundamentally severed; the tree no longer remains. This "wound" refers to the wound of doubt, namely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and the three poisons (*tri-viṣa*).
The Sūtra says: "Regarding the six sense-bases (*ṣadāyatana*), those who receive them suffer as if they were struck by three hundred boils; it is only that people do not perceive it.
Within a single person's body, there are altogether one thousand eight hundred [of these].
The "excrescence" refers to the eye receiving forms and the body experiencing suffering; this is the fault of the eye.
It is the same for all six sense organs, and thus they are innumerable.
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have already been understood and severed; they are like a tree that has been felled to the ground and can no longer stand upright.
Once dispersed, they do not manifest again.
This means that the five aggregates (*skandha*) and the six sense-fields (*āyatana*) have already been dissipated and no longer appear.
The original dharmas from whence they arose shall never arise again.
The phenomena of the five aggregates cease and are no longer reborn.
Those who maintain the precepts yet engage in deceptive trading fall into two categories:
first, those who fall due to craving; second, those who fail to avoid [craving] while maintaining the precepts yet engaging in deceptive trading.
One should employ the precepts to cultivate the Way, yet instead turns the mind toward seeking rebirth in the heavens; therefore, it is said that one does not understand how to avoid [this error].
Furthermore, the *Anban jie* states: "To turn the fundamental vows of the precepts and, instead of using the precepts to seek the Way, conversely seek the glory and pleasure of the heavens."
This is called the transformation of precepts.
Having originally vowed to seek the Way, yet deviating from the Way to follow worldly desires—such a regression no longer exists; therefore, it is called "exhaustion."

If you intend to follow this and restrain yourself by observing the precepts, from this you shall attain the state of a deva or one comparable to a deva; you shall dwell in the heavens. There, you will be known as "Armor," and a jade maiden shall dwell with you, and both shall enjoy each other's company. Such is your hope; such is it possible.
"It would be well; it would be well to dwell together in mutual delight with celestial jade maidens.
To thus form a bond through such thoughts and direct one's intention toward this is craving; even if one maintains the precepts, one falls into a state of delusion and trade.
Because they do not understand this, they maintain the precepts of a śrāmaṇera while engaging in bartering and trading.
Regarding what kind of precepts: for a śrāmaṇera, what constitutes the transgression of trading?
What is meant by "trading"?
It is for the sake of the mind-born being that one attains purity through precepts, attains liberation through precepts, and attains the essential through precepts;
it is for the sake of crossing over from suffering and pleasure. No longer undergoing the suffering and pleasure of sin and merit, one attains Nirvana.
Alternatively, if one seeks deliverance through the mind born of vows, this constitutes a lack of understanding; one merely maintains the precepts while engaging in further conceptual proliferation.

Having maintained the precepts, one should instead advance upward toward the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; yet, by halting at the precepts and seeking deliverance through mere aspiration, it is said that one does not "renounce."
For what reason is it said that one does not understand the transformation and exchange?
It is because the mind arises from clothing.
"Clothing" refers to the three Dharma robes of a bhikṣu.
One tradition states:
[This garment] serves as clothing for those in the heavens.
Furthermore, one attains transcendence through aspiration, and through suffering and pleasure, one achieves detachment.
This means to distance oneself from both pleasure and pain.
One should take these two types of karma as one's clothing and also wish to take them as one's mold.
What is meant by "mold"?

To think that these two types of precepts, robes, and vows will lead to liberation, that through them one will attain the essential, that through them one will transcend suffering and pleasure, and that through them one will attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by means of suffering and pleasure—this is an incorrect reckoning of the Dharma.
"Improper conceptualization" means taking what is false to be true.
It is not following the intention for liberation; rather, it is following what is improper for liberation, conceptualizing it as being correct, and thus proceeding accordingly with such existence.
Following these aforementioned practices, there is thus birth and death.
To tolerate, to find mental satisfaction, and to expect—these constitute fetters and views;
it is to tolerate birth and death.
The mind—this mind can be brought to celestial glory.
To view it in such a way is a fettered view, not the true view.
To act accordingly is liberation.
To seek liberation through views is not true liberation;
to fail to maintain the precepts and instead engage in worldly trade is the second fetter.
The disciples who have attained the Way have already abandoned [them]; those who say they have "already attained" mean they have abandoned the defilement of exchange.
This is because they are non-existent; their roots have already been severed.
There is no longer any basis for precepts or vows.

Once the tree has been uprooted and no longer appears, such that it will not grow again from behind, this is what constitutes purified precepts; like the precepts of one who has attained the Path, they follow the traces and are not broken.
Those who have already attained the Way are said to uphold the precepts without breaking or violating them.
"To break" means to leak;
it refers to a breach.
This means that one has already fully perfected the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, such that there are no leaks.

Furthermore, the *Anban Shouyi Jie* states: "Vigor lies in practice; when the beginning and end are joined together so that wrong thoughts cannot enter between them, this is called being without leaks."
This is what is meant by that.
There is no loss and no regret; there is only increase, as is the case for one who possesses wisdom.
To say "it is acceptable to the wise" means it is approved by those who possess wisdom.
There is nothing that can take it away.
That is to say, when one acts in accordance with the Dharma, nothing can take away one's resolve.
[If] one does not act in accordance with the Dharma, then one will not attain concentration.

To attain concentration from this state, there are these three fetters which the disciple on the path has already severed; having entered the track of the Dharma, he no longer falls into unwholesome states and is destined for liberation. Having seven more births remaining among gods and humans, his cycle of rebirths will come to an end.
This refers to the "Stream-enterer" (srotāpanna), who undergoes seven births and seven deaths.
Passing back and forth between the heavens and the human realm in this manner for seven cycles, they finally attain the stage of Arhatship.
It is said that the period of coming and going within the cycle of birth and death has reached its end.
One then attains the essential means for escaping suffering—escaping from suffering, escaping the triple world, and being freed from all forms of duḥkha.
There are four types of appropriate application, namely the four applications.
The first is the application of what has already been understood (*parijñāta-yoga*).
Having already understood suffering, it is said that the "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) has attained the Path.
Second is the application of abandonment through severance; third is the application of personal realization.
This refers to the "non-returner" (anāgāmin).
"Having exhausted suffering" refers to its complete severance.
The fourth is "correspondence through fulfillment," which refers to the Arhat (*arhat*),
meaning that [the path] has already been fully perfected.
That disciple of the Dharma and Vinaya is associated with the realization that suffering has been understood;
having realized that suffering has been understood, he is one who should understand the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
He is associated with the abandonment of the origin (*samudaya*) through its cessation; he is associated with the personal realization of its exhaustion (*nirodha*).

The "exhaustion of self-realization" refers to the realization of the exhaustion of the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the six sense-fields (*āyatanas*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
From the perspective of the Path, this constitutes the fulfillment of correspondence; therein, tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) proceed together in tandem.
This means that the four truths, tranquility (śamatha), and insight (vipaśyanā) all proceed together in a single location,
at a single time, and with a single mind;
in such a state of stillness, there is no [discursive] mind.
Originally there is this; there is an intention that causes it to perform four functions. What are these four?
First is suffering; having been liberated from suffering, it corresponds with suffering.
The second is cultivation (*bhāvanā*); having abandoned what was to be abandoned through cultivation, it is associated with cultivation.
The third is exhaustion (*kṣaya*); having personally realized exhaustion, it is associated with exhaustion.
The fourth is the path (*mārga*); by bringing the path to full development through the path, it is associated with the path.
For what reason is there association with the liberation from suffering?
For what reason is there association with the abandonment through the cessation of the origin?
For what reason is there association with the personal realization of cessation?
Why is this? Because it is associated with the path that has already been increased and fulfilled;
that is to say, it refers to being associated with the complete fulfillment of the Four Noble Truths.
There is a simile for this: it is like the movement of foam upon water, where one says that the water carries the foam across.
At the very top, there are four veins that extend from this shore to the further shore.
Reaching the further shore and crossing over, one severs these veins;
one severs the water-veins.
It is also like this: when *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are practiced together, in a single place, at one time, and with a single intention, one reaches the ultimate goal.
