This means that the practitioner uses the two swords of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to sever the channels of the twelve links of dependent origination, cutting off the flow to attain the Way.
The single place is nirvāṇa; likewise, the single time and the single intention are so as well.

To accomplish these four matters, it is like the rising of the sun reaching its zenith, which performs four functions: it brings forth light to destroy darkness, and it manifests forms to their ultimate extent.
These four matters serve as metaphors for the Four Noble Truths; their meaning is the same as that in the *Ānāpāna-smṛti*.
It is like crossing by boat: one leaves this shore and reaches the opposite shore.
This means that the Bodhisattva acts like a ferryman who brings people and goods to the other shore; the deliverance of the Bodhisattva is also like this.
He brings things to the point where their continuity is severed; the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is likewise carried out in tandem.

They arise together and proceed in unison; they share a single location, a single time, and a single intention. Their ultimate goal is to accomplish four tasks: to illuminate suffering according to its true characteristics so as to bring about its understanding; to sever the habitual tendencies (*anuśaya*) according to their appropriate correspondence; to realize the exhaustion [of outflows] through personal realization according to their appropriate resolution; and to cultivate the essentials of the Path according to their appropriate application.

Why is this? Because suffering corresponds to the liberation through direct experience; accumulation corresponds to the liberation through abandonment; cessation corresponds to the liberation through the realization of suffering; and the path corresponds to the essential liberation through practice.
Calm abiding and insight are also like this.

They proceed in tandem, in one place, at one time, and with one intention. Calm abiding must reach its ultimate limit for the sake of four matters: for the realization of suffering, for the abandonment of its origin, for the personal realization of its cessation, and for the fulfillment of the path.
For example, when a lamp or candle is lit, it performs four functions from beginning to end: it provides illumination, it dispels darkness, it reveals forms, and it removes doubt.
"Quelling" (què) means "eliminating.
It refers to the inability to resolve one's doubts; fire is able to eliminate them.
*Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are also like this, performing four functions: to recognize suffering (*duḥkha*) and to sever its origin (*samudaya*).

Having already attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one practices them no longer for the sake of mere knowledge, but for the sake of exhaustion through personal realization and for the sake of fulfilling the path.

It is like lighting a lamp; it possesses four purposes: to manifest light, to dispel darkness, to reveal forms, and to exhaust the oil and the wick. The uppermost of these, the purpose of the mind, likewise has four meanings.
Cessation and contemplation are likewise so.
The maladies of the world consist only of suffering and its accumulation;
the bliss of the Path consists of cessation and contemplation, which are like a lamp wick burning down until it is exhausted.

The two concurrent practices, occurring in one place, at one time, and with one intention, culminate in four tasks: to recognize suffering through its association with suffering; to abandon the origin through its association with the origin; to realize cessation through its association with cessation; and to cultivate the path through its association with the path.
For what reason is it associated with the suffering of suffering?
For what reason is it associated with the origin of the origin?
For what reason is it associated with the cessation of cessation through personal realization?
Why is this? Because it is for the sake of the path of exertion and the path of fulfillment;
from what should one respond?
From tranquility and insight.
What is the application?
How should it be maintained?
Having applied the mind to contemplation, one sees the five aggregates as suffering through that application of the mind.
That which is bound by the mind is *śamatha* (calm abiding); having already seen the five aggregates as suffering is *vipaśyanā* (insight).
This refers to the aforementioned analysis of the success and failure of the Four Noble Truths.
That which is so characterized is proximate to the five aggregates.
This refers to the five aggregates and the six sense faculties being mutually dependent and proximate.
They can give rise to desire and attachment; one may wish to continue this mutual association and not abandon their habitual practice, yet these [desires] have already been severed and exhausted.

The path of śamatha and vipaśyanā is also like this: it causes these dharmas of the Path and the Four Truths to be in one place, at one time, and with one intention, reaching the ultimate limit, so that the Four Truths may be brought into correspondence.

Regarding this path, when a disciple of the noble ones has understood these characteristics of phenomena as they truly are, this is called the stage of vision (*darśana-bhūmi*), for they have seen the track of the path.
Having attained the continuity of the path and reached the station of the track of the path, they further cultivate tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, he again repeatedly contemplates the increase of tranquility (*śamatha*),
so that the fetters of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of desire and ill-will may be further eliminated;
this is the path for the exhaustion of the latent tendency of craving for sensual pleasure.

The disciple who has attained the Way receives [the fruits of] coming and going; by this, his feet are supported. Having followed through with coming and going, he then destroys the root of suffering; this is the stage of attenuation (*tanubhūmi*). He has thus completed the merit of coming and going, and having arrived, he abides in virtue; he stops within the stopping of the Way and its virtue.

Furthermore, they increase their tranquility and insight, causing those who are driven by other forms of craving and hatred to achieve complete relinquishment; yet those driven by desire and hatred have not yet achieved complete relinquishment.
Because they have not yet achieved complete relinquishment, they are moved by the underlying tendencies and fetters, and immediately return to the darkness of the five aggregates.
He causes the fetters to be completed; once they are completed, he becomes a disciple who has attained the Way, having then untied and brought to completion the five fetters.

What are these five? First, the view that the body is either existent or non-existent; second, the resolution of doubt; third, being neither deluded nor wavering regarding the precepts; fourth, the absence of longing; and fifth, the absence of anger—these are the five fetters.
Having completed this, one becomes a disciple who has attained the Way and no longer returns to the world.

Having crossed over the world, they do not return to this world; this is called "receding from the ground. This is the attainment of the merit of non-return; having achieved the merit of non-return, one recedes from the ground—that is, one recedes from all grounds of evil.
The Non-returner (anāgāmin) refers to one who has attained the path therein and will no longer return to this world to undergo suffering in a physical body.
Furthermore, by augmenting the wings of śamatha and vipaśyanā, they bring about the relinquishment of the five higher fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
What are the five?
First is desire for form; second is desire for the formless; third is delusion; fourth is arrogance; and fifth is lack of understanding.

The above five aggregates being exhausted constitutes the abandonment of the five fetters; thus one is without attachment, has already transcended the world, and has brought an end to all outflows. Having attained liberation through the right path, this is called the completion of the ground. It is said that an Arhat dwells in the world like space; therefore, he is called "one without attachment."
The five higher fetters have all been extinguished; therefore, it is said that liberation is complete.

With no further attachment remaining, there is the wondrous state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Having completed this relinquishment, the life-faculty of the world comes to an end, and the suffering of the world is exhausted; thus, suffering shall not arise again.

He considers that these aggregates, bases, and elements have already been exhausted, are tranquil and non-existent, that the aggregates, bases, and elements are no longer linked, and will not arise again.
This has already been explained above in this sutra.
"Not connecting again" means being severed from the five aggregates (skandhas) and the six sense bases (āyatanas).
"Not arising again" means no longer giving rise to the five aggregates and the six sense bases; this is called "quiescence," and therefore it is said that they do not arise again.

This is called having completed the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it has already explained what corresponds to the Truths (*satya*), and it has also explained what corresponds to the Categories (*skandha*).
"Categories" refers to the four truths categorized by their constituents.
It also explains the stages (*bhūmi*).
The fourth is the ground;
it is also called merit and called abandonment.
It is the abandonment of all evils.
He speaks of transgression and speaks of renunciation; he speaks of the two unconditioned states. For all beings, he teaches in this way.
The Buddha has already completed his further crossing of the world; if anyone wishes to cross the world, they should follow this.
What are they? They are the nine successive meditative attainments of right concentration:

the four dhyānas, the four formless right concentrations, and the concentration of the cessation of perception and feeling; these constitute the nine successive meditative attainments of right concentration.
In that first dhyāna, one has already abandoned five kinds [of factors] corresponding to the five [hindrances].
What are these five that have been abandoned? They are the five hindrances (pañca-nīvaraṇāni):
First, sensual desire; second, ill will; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; fifth, doubt—these are the five.
Having attained the higher dhyānas, one has already abandoned those hindrances of sensual desire.
What is meant by the term "craving for sensual desires"?

It refers to that which causes one to set out toward attachment to the five kinds of pleasure, which arises from seeking according to one's wishes, and which initiates the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) without relinquishing them; this is called the hindrance of craving for sensual desires.
What is that hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*)?

When a person gives rise to and acts upon the characteristic of resentment and hatred, which is the root of unrighteousness (*adharma*), and from which one is driven and by which one is incited—this is called the hindrance of ill-will.
What is that hindrance of torpor and drowsiness?
Torpor is the settling of the body and the settling of the mind; it is the cessation of the body and the cessation of the mind.
This means that having attained the cessation of body and mind, one no longer follows after these five hindrances.

To be deluded regarding the body and deluded regarding the mind; to be heavy in body and heavy in mind; to be unsteady in body and unsteady in mind; to be unmanageable in body and unmanageable in mind—this is called sleepiness and torpor.
Why is this so? Because the mental characteristics follow one another, causing the state of darkness (*tamas*) to move and the state of motion (*rajas*) to move.
Until these are abandoned, they act as the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*); through their repeated movement, they reach the state of darkness.
Causing one to be unable to act is called *styāna* (torpor).
The former is *middha* (drowsiness) and the latter is *styāna*; together they are termed the hindrance of drowsiness and torpor (*styānamiddhanīvaraṇa*).
Because a hindrance covers the eyes like a film, causing the eyes to see nothing, it is called a "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*).
What is that which he does not understand regarding the hindrance of regret?
It is the non-restraint of the body with respect to regret. What is that?
When one thinks something is acceptable but later finds it unacceptable and cannot bring oneself to regret that [initial] state—
being unreflective at first and subsequently feeling regret— this is collectively termed the hindrance of unreflective regret (*apratyavekṣā-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*).
What is that hindrance of doubt?
It is the assembly of those who do not have faith in the Buddha, do not have faith in the Dharma, and do not have faith in the Saṅgha.
"Saṅgha" refers to the community of bhikṣus.
Not understanding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path [to its cessation] refers to the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
"Refers to" (*bi*) means that there are numerous fetters;
"refers to" (*bi*) also implies succession.
It also arises from this, which is called the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*).

There are likewise five kinds of doubt: there is the doubt concerning local districts (*kheṭaka*), which refers to the many people in a commandery or district who speak of the Path differently, causing the doubter’s mind to be uncertain.

There is doubt regarding the arousal of verbal teachings, and there is doubt regarding the differentiation of the Path; this refers to the doubt that because people give different oral instructions, they are therefore uncertain.
There is doubt regarding the desire for meditative concentration, and there is doubt regarding the blessings obtained through the Path.
Thus, this is called the explanation of fixed doubt.
These are the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*).
Regarding these five hindrances, the verses and phrases have already been explained above by the Superior One (*uttara-puruṣa*).
The *Buddhakaṣa-rāja-sūtra* also speaks of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*):
first, lust; second, anger; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; and fifth, doubt.
The mind that does not cease is essentially the same as this.
Why is this so? It is because it serves as an antidote.
They obstruct all pure dharmas. How do they obstruct? Lust obstructs purity;

hatred obstructs equanimity; sleep obstructs tranquility; lethargy obstructs diligence; the five pleasures obstruct joy; furthermore, attachment obstructs non-regret; doubt obstructs wisdom; and ignorance of the origin obstructs clear understanding.
Because one is not deluded by the five hindrances, it is called "clear understanding.
From the *Śrī-garbha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, Scroll II, "The Buddha’s Teaching on the Seal of Wisdom," Chapter 163: "One should know, Śāriputra, that this is the explanation of meditative concentration."
The body of the Tathāgata is a non-body; it is without action, without arising, without cessation,
without origin, never created, without conjunction, without wandering, without arrival, without cognition,
without cultivation, entirely pure, without accumulation, without aversion, without movement, without stopping, and without birth.
Without retribution, without vision, without interval, without odor, without taste, without touch, without consciousness,
without clarity, without analogy, without cognitive patience, without aspiration, without thought, not the mind, detached from the mind,
with a mind that is equanimous yet without equanimity, with the mind departed, without anything to be given, and without the five destinies. The five.

The Way’s severance must be complete: without enclosure, without affliction, without existence, without fear, without the acceptable or unacceptable, without karma, without accomplishment, without speech, without the unmanifesting of softness, neither light nor dark, neither extinction nor non-extinction, having departed from extinction yet already extinguished;
it is pure, supremely pure, and that purity is not employed.
Neither pleasant nor dear; neither burdened nor free from burden; already abiding in the state of nowhere; neither departing, nor dying, nor perishing;
neither dharma nor non-dharma; neither land nor no-land; not exhausted, there being no exhaustion;
having abandoned exhaustion; without anger; detached from heaven, detached from sound, and detached from speech.
Free from volition, neither conjoined nor disjoined, neither extreme nor non-extreme, neither departing nor not departing,
neither dual nor non-delightful; without that which is felt, without that which is seen,
without characteristics and free from characteristics, not seeking the clarity of characteristics, serene and unhurried, unattached and detached from attachment, establishing faith without duality.

It is as when one examines thoroughly and examines according to the meaning: not failing those who seek help, delivering those who have not crossed over, removing that which has not been removed, saving those who have not been saved, speaking that which has not been spoken;

it is equal to non-duality, equal to the incomparable, equal to emptiness, equal to the placeless, equal to the unborn, equal to the unattainable, without rest and free from cessation, already quiescent.
It is quiescent, fully quiescent, and dispersedly liberated; it is the excellence of mental conduct, the turning toward the essential, and the severance of all retribution.
It is perfected as the ultimate truth; its physical manifestation is luminous and pure.
It is without self-reflection, without the practice of active engagement, and liberated from liberation itself. It is non-responsive, not level, not long, not round, and not square.
It praises the aggregates (skandhas), does not name the elements (dhātus), does not extol the sense-bases (āyatanas); it is not a number, nor is it brought into calculation;
it is not subject to rebirth, is invisible, and is neither known nor dead; it is not a worldly cause, yet there is no non-cause;
its body is thus without falling away and has no dwelling place; it is neither end nor beginning, neither thought nor sorrow.
This matter is not a dispute, not a sign of evil, not extinction, not cessation, not something created,
